title: Tax Incentives and the Decision to Purchase Health Insurance: Evidence from the Self-Employed
research_question: How does the after-tax price of health insurance affect an individual's decision to purchase health insurance coverage? Specifically, what is the price sensitivity of the discrete choice to be insured among self-employed workers when tax-based subsidies alter the relative cost of insurance versus paying medical expenses out of pocket?
data_description: The primary data come from the March Current Population Survey (CPS), a nationally representative household survey of over 50,000 households that collects retrospective information on health insurance coverage, employment status, job characteristics, and income for the prior calendar year. The authors pool the March 1986 and 1987 CPS files (covering insurance status in 1985-1986) and the March 1989 and 1990 files (covering 1988-1989), excluding 1987. The unit of observation is the individual aged 25-54. Key variables include private health insurance coverage, self-employment status (with at least $2,000 in self-employment income), wage and salary income, family/tax-unit income, marital status, education, experience, gender, race, hours and weeks worked, industry, and occupation. Imputed marginal tax rates and after-tax insurance prices are constructed using the NBER TAXSIM calculator, the Treasury Individual Tax Model, and 1977 National Medical Care Expenditure Survey data. Supplementary checks use the 1984 and 1986 SIPP panels.
institutional_context: Prior to the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA86), employer-provided health insurance was excluded from employees' taxable income and payroll tax base, while self-employed individuals who did not itemize had to pay for health insurance with after-tax dollars and received no comparable tax benefit. TRA86 introduced a new tax provision allowing self-employed workers to deduct 25 percent of their health insurance premiums from taxable income, partially equalizing the tax treatment of insurance across employment types. The reform also lowered marginal income tax rates substantially (the top rate fell from 50 to 28 percent), raised the AGI floor for itemizing medical expenses from 5 to 7.5 percent, and increased the standard deduction. These combined changes meaningfully reduced the after-tax price of insurance for the self-employed, especially higher-income self-employed taxpayers, while leaving the after-tax price for employed workers roughly unchanged, creating differential incentives across groups.
